title: Diary of a Country Priest (1951, Bresson): A Film of Unrelenting Power

commenti.body:
I would dearly love to see this, but the only physical release in the US; a DVD from Criterion, is OOP. As far as I know it's not available in HiDef.

It was one of Tarkovsky's favourite films.

My feeling is that this is the beginning of the loner-as-existential-hero theme that would become so important later. There has been something similar before in the noir hard-boiled detective, but Bresson brings this figure from crime drama to domestic drama so that Country Priest could be thought of almost as a spiritual noir. 

This is extracted from my substack piece on [Diary of a Country Priest as compared with First Reformed](https://apmurphy.substack.com/p/back-to-back-7-priest-hole)  


>The priest has the "Holy Agony" which is not a physical ailment, though he has plenty of those too, but an existential crisis of faith. This means he can deliver what he calls "the miracle of Empty Hands", which is where someone who is in deep despair can actually comfort and console someone else but receive no personal gratification for doing so. The miracle allows him to bring one of his parishoners back from an abyss of bitterness, but leaves him much worse off as a result...  
  
Though characterised as conservative, Bresson's style is designed to be radically liberating. He felt that by using the cinematic craft to manipulate the viewer's thoughts and emotions, cinema as commonly practised created fake feelings, shallow and easily forgotten. By paring away all that manipulation, above all the emotionalism of acting, Bresson believed the story itself could create a deeper and more profound realisation combining thought and feeling. Something like that impulse would go on to motivate the French New Wave, thoroughgoing atheists though most of them were.
